core_idea: The Angel of the Lord in the Old Testament is a distinct divine figure, identified as the pre-incarnate Son of God (Christ), who appears as Yahweh's messenger and acts as the commander of God's armies, leading and protecting Israel.

segments.reason: Introduces the topic: the Angel of the Lord is a fuzzy figure for many Christians, and the episode will clarify his identity and nature.
Linguistic analysis: 'the Angel of the Lord' (Ha Malak Yahweh) uses a definite article, indicating a particular being, not just any angel.

Two valid readings of 'of': possessive (Yahweh's angel) and attributive (Yahweh angel). The latter leads to Second Temple literature where an angel is named Yeho-El (Yahweh God), showing a divine figure.
Ancient Jews were not unitary monotheists; they believed in a divine figure distinct from God the Father, which is necessary to understand the Angel of the Lord.
The Angel of the Lord is an especially divine figure, connected to messianic traditions (e.g., Isaiah 9:6 'Angel of Great Counsel').
New Testament references (Acts 7:53, Hebrews 2:2, Galatians 3:19-20) show the Torah was given through angels, with a singular intermediary identified as the Angel of the Presence (Christ).
Exodus 33:11 and 33:20 present a seeming contradiction: Yahweh speaks to Moses face to face, yet says no one can see His face. This is resolved by recognizing two hypostases within the one God.
The contradiction in Exodus reveals a second figure who is Yahweh but distinct from the unseen Father. This is the Angel of the Lord, a pre-incarnate Christ.
Answer to caller: The Angel of the Lord is the second person of the Trinity in a post-resurrectional body, because Christ is incarnate without change and eternal realities transcend time.
Exodus 23:20-21: God sends an angel with His name in him, who will not pardon transgression. This angel is the same as the Angel of the Presence who gave the Torah.
The 'name' in the angel means God's identity, not the tetragrammaton. This identifies the angel as bearing God's own identity.
The sign of the Spirit descending and remaining (John 1:33) identifies Jesus as the one in whom God's name dwells, paralleling the Angel of the Lord in Exodus.
Exodus 14:19-20: The Angel of God moves behind Israel at the Red Sea, with the pillar of cloud (Holy Spirit). This shows the Trinity acting together.
Jude 5: Jesus saved a people out of Egypt. This directly identifies the Angel of the Lord as Christ.
Exodus 23:22: Obeying the angel's voice is equated with obeying God. The Father and the Angel are completely united in will and action.
The Angel leads Israel to conquer the giant clans (Amorites, Hittites, etc.), showing his role as commander of God's armies in gigantomachy.
Joshua 5:13-15: The commander of the Lord's army appears with a drawn sword, receives worship, and declares the ground holy—identifying him as the Angel of the Lord (Christ), not St. Michael.
Three details identify the commander as the Angel of the Lord: drawn sword (used elsewhere for the Angel and Yahweh), acceptance of worship, and the command to remove sandals (as in Exodus 3).
Judges 2:1-5: The Angel of the Lord speaks in first person as Yahweh, saying 'I brought you up from Egypt' and 'I will never break my covenant.' This shows his divine identity.
Exodus 3:2-6: The Angel of the Lord appears in the burning bush, and God calls to Moses. The Angel is identified as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Judges 6: The Angel of the Lord appears to Gideon, and the text alternates between 'Angel of Yahweh' and 'Yahweh,' showing their identity.
Summary: The Angel of the Lord leads armies, protects Israel, punishes, and defeats enemies. This is the Son of God with a drawn sword.
The Angel's warrior role is not a contradiction with Jesus' humility; Jesus could call legions of angels but chose to offer himself. This is a 'special ops' mission to defeat death.
Conclusion: Christ is actively present in the Old Testament as the Angel of the Lord. This challenges modern individualism and shows that eternal reality is more real than our daily struggles.
